summary: This article explains how mapmakers turn the round Earth into flat, useful maps using projections, symbols, legends, scale, and different map types.
introduce: Write “Alike” and “Different” at the top of a T-chart on the board and ask students to compare two school subjects in one minute. Explain that “Maps: Representing the World on Paper” asks them to make the same kind of comparison.

keyTerms.def: a shape that is perfectly round in every direction, like a ball
a difficult problem that takes effort or skill to solve
to pull something so it becomes longer or more spread out than it was

challengeTerms.def: a person whose job is to design and draw maps
a mathematical method for turning a round surface into a flat map
a change that makes something's shape, size, or position slightly inaccurate

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that a map does not need to be perfectly accurate to still be useful? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Explain why a flat map of the world can never be perfectly accurate.
struggling: Read the first part of the article aloud together, review sphere, challenge, and stretch, and let weak readers fill in a T-chart of alike and different with sentence starters.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use cartographer, projection, and distortion in a short paragraph that compares two ideas from the article and explain which difference matters most.
